accuracy.evidence: Checked against DfE Development Matters 2021 (3 and 4 year olds: understand a question or instruction that has two parts), the EYFS characteristics of effective learning and the Listening, Attention and Understanding early learning goal (ask questions to clarify understanding), Head Start ELOF Approaches to Learning (initiative and curiosity), and Chouinard (2007) on preschoolers' information-seeking questions. Naming versus procedural questions and the two-part instruction length are stated as those sources describe them.

misconceptions.evidence: The lab answers each documented slip for this age: asking 'How do I do it?' when a name is needed (and the reverse) gets a message naming which kind of question fits; 'I give up' gets 'you never find out'; tapping steps in the wrong order replays the heard order; choosing teddy, the cat, the fish or the plant is told they cannot talk back. Prediction 1 targets trying harder instead of asking, prediction 2 targets grabbing before listening.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfind is built around one loop that only this topic has: a gap (unknown name or a job I cannot do), a question card dragged to a helper, then the helper's two- or three-step answer that the child must carry out in the heard order. flagask (ages 4-6) is about asking instead of guessing a box and asking again kindly, flaghelp is a help ladder and flagqw maps question words onto a picture; none makes the child act on the answer. The shingle gate passed against every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child only learns the hedgehog, kite and magnet names by asking the naming question, and only opens the jar, zips the coat and builds the tower by asking how and then doing the steps in order, so the finding-out comes from the action; the done messages confirm it ('Asking works when you listen and try'). The mixed step makes the child decide which question each new thing needs.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Keep pulling hard' for a jar that will not open, before three jobs are solved by asking how; and 'Grab it and do it my way' before the steps task, where the wrong order is rejected and the heard order works. The done message quotes the child's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with tagged wrong answers, each with its own correction: asked how instead of what, guessed, asked what when stuck on a boot, gave up, ran off after asking, kept asking the same thing, asked teddy, asked the tree, did Gran's second step first, and thought order does not matter.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores FK -0.6 against the family limit of 5.0 with sentences like 'Hold first. Twist next.' Adult text scores FK 6.5 against 10 and still uses the precise terms characteristics of effective learning, two-part instruction, information-seeking question, naming question and procedural question.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed. Each kid paragraph models one real ask-listen-try moment, each adult paragraph carries curriculum, method, named mistakes or the lab outline, and explanation overlap with Asking Questions (lesson 165) and every other lesson stays under the 12 percent limit.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 in light and dark show the child, the thing and the helper box in one row, three question cards across the bottom with wrapped labels, step tiles big enough for a thumb and the speech bubble wrapping inside the canvas; the button twins sit below. walk.cjs completed all five Show me tasks on desktop and iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme on desktop or iPhone and there were no console errors. Every drag has a button twin (the three question buttons, named step buttons, named helper buttons), the young class gives 56 px targets, and the canvas aria-label speaks each answer, e.g. 'Listen again: first hold the jar, then twist the lid.'

sources: DfE (2021) Development Matters: Communication and Language and Characteristics of Effective Learning, 3 and 4 year olds
DfE (2024) EYFS statutory framework: ELG Listening, Attention and Understanding
Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework (ELOF): Approaches to Learning, initiative and curiosity
Chouinard, M. M. (2007). Children's questions: a mechanism for cognitive development. Monographs of the SRCD 72(1)
